title: Recapping the recent Pokemon TCG PH Controversy

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The recent controversy surrounding the Pokemon TCG community has renewed conversation on safe spaces.

You’re walking around an event, happy to see your hobby out in full display. With how frequently hobby gatherings and events have been happening, it’s no surprise that these interests would eventually be monetized one way or another. Communities form, guards come down, and a sense of familiarity takes over.

You’d think the hobby space was safe, seeing the same vendors over and over again across a variety of events. But what happens when that familiarity is challenged? All the trust and goodwill established over months, possibly even years, can come crashing down when allegations of inappropriate behavior involving a familiar vendor come to light.
What happened in the Filipino Pokemon TCG space?

Recently, an ongoing controversy involving seller Jaime “TipsyJ” Tolentino began circulating on the Pokémon TCG Philippines subreddit, originating from a thread warning the community about his alleged predatory behavior.

The discussion stemmed from leaked group chat messages that reportedly showed multiple instances of inappropriate conduct, including alleged gestures toward a woman wearing shorts and inappropriate attention toward a minor wearing a Gengar jacket.
Another member of the group chat, “1MPIRE”, was also criticized for allegedly objectifying women in his immediate vicinity.

Following the circulation of these messages, local event organizer MNL Card Convention removed TipsyJ as a vendor and sponsor from its event. As more individuals began speaking out about the allegations, others came to his defense.

However, members of the community questioned these defenses, noting the apparent connections between the individuals involved and the same vendor circle. Several members of that circle subsequently faced criticism and calls for boycotts over their alleged involvement or enabling behavior.

With discussions about TipsyJ spreading across Reddit and Facebook, another vendor and then moderator of the Facebook group Pokemon Collectors Group PH Buy & Sell 🇵🇭 (TCG & More), “Tondo Cartel”, also became involved in the controversy after allegedly seeking ways to trace the IP addresses of anonymous Reddit users.
As updates continued to circulate, the situation eventually caught the attention of international TCG content creators.
What might otherwise have remained a localized hobby controversy reached an international audience when American TCG content creator and patent attorney “UMU” took notice of the situation.
After sharing a screenshot of a Reddit thread featuring an apology from “Tondo Cartel” that drew criticism from community members, the vendor subsequently threatened legal action against “UMU.”

Following allegations of attempts to identify anonymous users, discussions about Reddit IP tracing, and legal threats against individuals commenting on the controversy, both “Tondo Cartel” and TipsyJ eventually issued apologies.
Despite this, members of the community continued to call for accountability, with questions remaining about the conduct of those involved and how the situation was handled.

Making a living out of a hobby
The hobby space is filled with opportunities for monetization, with content creators and resellers being just a small part of an economic ecosystem that helps drive its growth.
With Pokémon being the franchise that it is, there’s no doubt that people across different age groups and backgrounds would find something to appreciate, making it a community with a diverse fanbase.

As interest grows, financial opportunities naturally follow, turning something that was once purely recreational into a potential business. In the collectibles space, for example, randomly collecting items growing up would bring a certain excitement whenever you found something that aligned with your interests. However, the dynamic changes when money gets involved.

That collectible you once had multiples of growing up could eventually become a retro commodity with its own market value. What starts as an opportunity to sell a few items can eventually turn into something bigger.

As capital grows with each sale and childhood collections are gradually liquidated, the doors to running an entire buy-and-sell business open up. It gets even more involved once importing products and establishing supplier relationships enter the picture, taking things further away from simply being a hobby.

Of course, turning a hobby into a business isn’t always the end goal. Plenty of individuals remain in their respective communities simply because they enjoy collecting, playing, or meeting people who share their interests.
However, the growing commercial side of these hobbies can also make it increasingly difficult for newcomers to participate.

Pokémon, for example, has been around for three decades and continues to enjoy widespread recognition. Yet with scalping, rising collectible prices, and other market factors, getting younger players into the physical trading card game can be a challenge.

While mobile alternatives such as Pokémon TCG Pocket provide another way to experience the franchise, there’s still something meaningful about owning and playing with physical cards featuring your favorite Pokémon.
There’s nothing inherently wrong with collectibles maintaining their value, nor is there anything wrong with people making a living out of their interests.

However, when the cost of participating becomes a barrier for younger audiences, it raises questions about accessibility and the future of the hobby. After all, children are among the very audiences that Pokémon continues to appeal to, and keeping the game accessible to them should remain part of the conversation.
Maintaining a safe space in the hobby scene
The TCG space has always had its share of bad actors, but seeing allegations of this nature emerge within a hobby that attracts younger audiences is particularly disappointing.

Beyond the accusations involving TipsyJ, the controversy also raises questions about the applicability of Republic Act No. 11313, or the Safe Spaces Act, particularly its provisions concerning gender-based sexual harassment in public spaces and online. Determining whether specific acts constitute violations of the law, however, would require further investigation.
Despite the controversy, the community response does offer some hope. Seeing individuals speak out, question questionable behavior, and demand accountability is something worth commending.

However, identifying bad actors and addressing misconduct should not fall solely on community members. Event organizers and vendors also have a responsibility to establish standards of conduct, particularly when their events attract younger audiences.
While the Philippine TCG events scene continues to grow, maintaining a welcoming environment should be just as important as expanding its commercial opportunities.

Organizers should have accessible channels for reporting misconduct, vendors should be held to consistent standards, and individuals who raise legitimate concerns should not have to worry about intimidation or retaliation.

There may be legitimate sellers who find themselves caught in the crossfire, but that shouldn’t discourage the community from asking questions and exercising caution. Supporting your local game store, attending events, and trying out the game should remain enjoyable experiences rather than something people have to approach with apprehension.

Sometimes, the magic is in the gathering, and the monetary aspect becomes less important. It’s having that safe space that makes hobbies enjoyable, especially when you’re surrounded by people who share the same passion and enthusiasm.

Not everyone could catch them all, but if there’s anything worth celebrating about this controversy, it’s seeing a community band together to protect the very thing that brought them together in the first place.
